source.title: Pretraining Curricula Enable Selective Fine-tuning
source.authors: Sebastian A. Bruijns; Jirko Rubruck; Mia Whitefield; Kai J. Sandbrink; Fazl Barez; Christopher Summerfield

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses safety fine-tuning and overrefusal, but its experiments use synthetic task refusal and rule-following in small transformers. They do not test harmful-request compliance in safety-trained chat models, response-position KL, compliant prefixes, or the other claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on synthetic task refusal and rule-following, not the harmful-request behavior or token-position mechanisms named by the claim versions. Those adjacent findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Statements about prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The experiments use small synthetic transformers (copy-first/copy-last ICL task; rule-based synthetic language task) with refusal deliberately trained via a refusal token, and 'alignment' defined as rule satisfaction. No safety-trained chat model, harmful request, harmful or benign fine-tuning attack, per-position KL, prefill/suffix attack, safety-weight localization, or deepening intervention is studied. Qi et al. 2406.05946 is cited only in related work. Results bear on overrefusal/selectivity of fine-tuning, a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct in substance. The authors also claim mechanistic support: imbalanced curricula yield disentangled task circuits and more L1-localized rule processing, refusal fine-tuning co-opts existing circuits, and early training has lasting effects fine-tuning cannot easily reverse. They note relevance to larger models is unclear.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares balanced and imbalanced pretraining curricula in synthetic task and rule-learning settings, then evaluates selective refusal fine-tuning or aligned-data fine-tuning. It does not use the original harmful-example fine-tuning, benign chat-data, KL-by-response-position, or compliant-prefill procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with pretraining curriculum and evaluation type: balanced versus imbalanced curricula differ in synthetic-task overrefusal and elicitation behavior, while post-fine-tuning free-generation misalignment is reported as nearly the same.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic copy task, refusal fine-tuning spills over onto the kept task after balanced pretraining but stays low after imbalanced pretraining; overrefusal correlates with circuit specialization (r = -0.70, 2-layer; r = -0.21, 4-layer).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining curriculum shapes task entanglement, which governs how selectively refusal fine-tuning can suppress one behaviour without overrefusal.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic rule-language task, aligned-only fine-tuning makes free generations near-zero misaligned for both curricula, but elicitation prompts reveal higher residual misalignment after balanced pretraining; early high-misalignment exposure (reverse curriculum) is not undone by fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning can produce surface-level alignment that masks unremoved misaligned tendencies, depending on pretraining data order.

record.problems: The main evidence comes from small, synthetic transformer tasks rather than chat models or harmful requests. The authors note that relevance to larger models is unclear. The refusal-rate figures describe standard deviations across seeds but do not provide numeric values in the text; balanced refusal analyses include only seeds that first achieve at least 90% accuracy on both tasks.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning of safety-trained models and harmful compliance.
Benign fine-tuning eroding safety in chat models.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes, or decoding attacks on refusal.
Localization of safety in few weights or ranks in safety-trained LLMs; the study localizes synthetic task circuits and rule processing in toy models only.
Whether safety data or objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Training that deepens safety beyond initial tokens and its robustness.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. All rows are toy-model synthetic results with values only in figures. The elicitation-vs-free-generation gap is thematically adjacent to shallow alignment but does not measure harmful compliance or token-position depth.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance in safety-trained chat models.
Benign-data fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance in safety-trained chat models.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes on harmful requests.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior; the paper studies synthetic-task circuits, not localized safety weights or ranks.
Whether safety training data or objectives cause first-token shallowness.
Training to spread safety behavior beyond initial response tokens and its robustness.

rows.check: State 'partial' is misleading: the measure is P(Misaligned) under elicitation, and the text reports balanced models have significantly higher misalignment than imbalanced after fine-tuning. Relative to the study's own comparison the effect (more residual misalignment) is observed; no numeric values given. Bears on no version.
